claim: For the two-player binary extraction game with payoff \(u_i(h_i,h_j)=b h_i-L\Pr(\Theta_t\le h_i+h_j)\), \(L>0\), \(b/L=19/50\), and threshold law \((\Pr(\Theta_t=1),\Pr(\Theta_t=2),\Pr(\Theta_t=3),\Pr(\Theta_t=4))=(2/5-t,1/10+3t,3/10-3t,1/5+t)\) for \(0\le t\le1/10\), every law has mean \(23/10\) and variance \(141/100\), yet the game is coordination for \(0\le t<1/50\), a strict Prisoner’s Dilemma for \(1/50<t<7/75\), and anti-coordination for \(7/75<t\le1/10\), with best-response ties at the two boundary values.

correctness.rationale: The law is a probability distribution on the full stated interval. Exact algebra gives constant mean 23/10, second moment 67/10, and variance 141/100. Best-response differences are \(L(r-p_1)\) and \(L(r-p_2)\); their signs yield coordination, strict Prisoner’s Dilemma, and anti-coordination on the stated intervals, with ties exactly at \(1/50\) and \(7/75\). A rational-arithmetic script checks the identities at boundary and interior points; the symbolic inequalities, not the tests, prove the full intervals.

value.rationale: The equilibrium regime changes the interpretation of conservation incentives: coordination, dominant extraction, and anti-coordination require different policy responses. The exact family shows that even exact knowledge of the threshold mean and variance does not identify the regime, so distributional information at action-relevant cutoffs can matter. This is a motivated structural counterexample, not a claim of empirical prediction or a routine numerical recomputation.
